name: DynamoDBFetch
title: DynamoDB Fetch
description: Fetch a record from an AWS DynamoDB table by key
whenToUse: Pick to read ONE DynamoDB record by its primary key, with an optional sort key. It emits the item and a found flag, so a miss is an answer rather than an error. Writing a record, and querying a range of them, are different jobs.

inputs.name: signal
inputs.description: Carries the key values, read under the field names named in config

outputs.name: output
outputs.description: The record, or null when nothing exists at that key

outputs.name: found
outputs.description: Whether an item existed at that key

tableName.title: Table Name
tableName.description: The DynamoDB table to read from

primaryKey.title: Primary Key Field
primaryKey.description: Field name of the partition key, looked up on the incoming signal

sortKey.title: Sort Key Field
sortKey.description: Field name of the sort key, if the table has one

authRequired.title: Require sign-in
authRequired.description: Only a signed-in caller may run this step. Leave off and it runs for whoever the workflow's trigger admitted, which is the usual answer.

authRole.title: Require role
authRole.description: A claim the caller's account must carry, as noun:verb (finance:approve, payments:refund). Leave blank to require only that they are signed in.

package.name: aws-dynamodb
package.packageFile:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/package.schema.json

# THE FIRST AWS PACKAGE AS MANIFESTS, and what proves `awsSigV4`.
#
# DynamoDB's HTTP API is one endpoint per region, an `X-Amz-Target` header naming the
# operation, and a JSON body. There is nothing else to it: take the signer and the
# translator out of @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb and that is what remains. The client, its
# cache and its four Command classes collapse into one call per node.
#
# TWO EXECUTOR CAPABILITIES CARRY IT, both using AWS's own libraries rather than anything
# written here:
#   awsSigV4              signs the request (@smithy/signature-v4)
#   encoding: dynamodbJson  translates values to and from DynamoDB's type tags
#                         (@aws-sdk/util-dynamodb, the same translator the DocumentClient
#                         uses). It cannot be an expression: the walk is recursive.
#
# The retired TypeScript is at `_legacy/nodes/aws-dynamodb/`.

name: aws-dynamodb
displayName: AWS DynamoDB
description: Read and write records in AWS DynamoDB
version: 2.0.0
category: storage
logoUrl: https://res.cloudinary.com/sonik/image/upload/v1751473913/gravity/icons/DynamoDB.png

features:
  - Put a record, read one by key
  - Query and scan on demand over a service edge
  - Signed with AWS Signature Version 4, no SDK in the node

# Regional endpoints, one subdomain level: dynamodb.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com.
allowedHosts:
  - "**.amazonaws.com"

requires:
  credential: [awsSigV4]
  transport: [json]
  executorVersion: ">=1.2.0"

credentials.awsCredential.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/credential.schema.json

# Transcribed from plugin-base's shared AWSCredential, NAME AND FIELDS UNCHANGED so
# credentials already stored against `awsCredential` keep resolving. Every AWS package
# shares this one, exactly as they shared the TypeScript definition.
#
# sessionToken is NEW, and additive. The retired definition had no such field, so anyone on
# temporary credentials (an assumed role, anything via STS) could not use these nodes at
# all. The signer sends and signs it only when it is filled in.

name: awsCredential
displayName: AWS Credentials
description: AWS credentials for AWS services (DynamoDB, S3, Bedrock, and the rest)
documentationUrl: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html

properties:
  - name: accessKeyId
    displayName: Access Key ID
    type: string
    required: true
    secret: true
    description: Your AWS Access Key ID
    placeholder: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
  - name: secretAccessKey
    displayName: Secret Access Key
    type: string
    required: true
    secret: true
    description: Your AWS Secret Access Key
    placeholder: ""
  - name: region
    displayName: AWS Region
    type: string
    secret: false # Public: it appears in every AWS endpoint hostname.
    required: false
    default: us-east-1
    description: The region your tables live in
    placeholder: us-east-1
  - name: sessionToken
    displayName: Session Token
    type: string
    required: false
    secret: true
    description: Only for temporary credentials from STS or an assumed role. Leave empty for a long-lived key.
    placeholder: ""

shared.dynamodb.yaml:
# The one call shape every DynamoDB operation shares.
#
# There is no per-operation URL: everything goes to the regional endpoint and the
# `X-Amz-Target` header picks the operation. A node $refs this and adds that header plus a
# body, which is why these manifests read like RPC rather than REST.

call: &call
  method: POST
  url: "return 'https://dynamodb.' + credentials.awsCredential.region + '.amazonaws.com/'"

  credential:
    scheme: awsSigV4
    service: dynamodb

  headers:
    # AWS's own JSON dialect, NOT application/json. The wrong one is a 400 that complains
    # about the body rather than the header, which sends you looking in the wrong place.
    Content-Type: application/x-amz-json-1.0

  transport: json
  # Plain JSON in the manifest; type tags on the wire. See api.schema.json#encoding.
  encoding: dynamodbJson

  retry:
    attempts: 3
    backoff: exponential
    # DynamoDB reports throttling as a 400 with a specific error type, not a 429. A blanket
    # 400 retry would resend genuinely malformed requests forever, so only the server-side
    # statuses are retried and a throughput problem surfaces instead of being hidden.
    on: [500, 502, 503, 504]

files.api/events.yaml:
# One row per output connector, in interface.yaml order.
#
# GetItem answers a MISS with a 200 and no `Item` key, which is the right shape: "nothing
# is stored there" is an answer, not a failure. Both rows read that same absence.

- emit: output
  from: response
  value: "return response.Item || null"

- emit: found
  from: response
  value: "return !!response.Item"
files.api/run.yaml:
# One signed GetItem. The key is built as PLAIN values; the encoding adds the type tags.

- $ref: dynamodb#call
  name: item
  headers:
    X-Amz-Target: DynamoDB_20120810.GetItem
    Content-Type: application/x-amz-json-1.0

  body:
    TableName: "{{ config.tableName }}"
    # Only the keys actually present go in. Sending a key whose value is undefined is a
    # validation error from DynamoDB, and a table with no sort key must not receive one.
    Key: >-
      return Object.fromEntries([]
        .concat(config.primaryKey && signal[config.primaryKey] !== undefined
          ? [[config.primaryKey, signal[config.primaryKey]]] : [])
        .concat(config.sortKey && signal[config.sortKey] !== undefined
          ? [[config.sortKey, signal[config.sortKey]]] : []))
files.config.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/config.schema.json

configSchema:
  type: object
  required: [tableName, primaryKey]
  properties:
    tableName:
      type: string
      title: Table Name
      description: The DynamoDB table to read from
      default: ""
      "ui:field": template
    # These name FIELDS, not values. The value is read off the incoming signal under that
    # name, which is how the retired node worked and what saved workflows expect.
    primaryKey:
      type: string
      title: Primary Key Field
      description: Field name of the partition key, looked up on the incoming signal
      default: universalId
      "ui:field": template
    sortKey:
      type: string
      title: Sort Key Field
      description: Field name of the sort key, if the table has one
      default: ""
      "ui:field": template
"ui:order": [tableName, primaryKey, sortKey]
files.interface.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/interface.schema.json

inputs:
  - name: signal
    type: object
    description: Carries the key values, read under the field names named in config
    required: false

outputs:
  - name: output
    type: object
    description: The record, or null when nothing exists at that key
  - name: found
    type: boolean
    description: Whether an item existed at that key

credentials:
  - name: awsCredential
    required: true
    displayName: AWS
files.node.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/node.schema.json

type: DynamoDBFetch
kind: PromiseNode

name: DynamoDB Fetch
category: Storage & Data
color: "#FF9900"

description: Fetch a record from an AWS DynamoDB table by key

whenToUse: >-
  Pick to read ONE DynamoDB record by its primary key, with an optional sort key. It emits
  the item and a found flag, so a miss is an answer rather than an error. Writing a record,
  and querying a range of them, are different jobs.

# WHO MAY RUN THIS (DECLARATIVE_NODES.md §9.13). Compulsory on every node, so that a node
# nobody thought about cannot look the same as one deliberately left open.
#
# `required: false` adds no requirement of its own: the node runs for whoever the trigger
# admitted. The trigger instance's publicEntry toggle still owns the door, and requirements
# only ever narrow.
auth:
  required: false

capabilities:
  # NOT cacheable. An item is exactly the kind of thing that changes underneath a workflow,
  # and a keyed read is cheap, so reuse buys little and can be wrong.
  cacheable: false
files.test.yaml:
$schema: https://docs.unoverse.ai/schemas/nodes/test.schema.json

# Reads back what the DynamoDB (put) fixture writes, so run that one first.

testData:
  config:
    tableName: Users
    primaryKey: universalId
    sortKey: ""
  inputs:
    signal:
      universalId: user-1001
  expect:
    # PLAIN values, not type tags: proving the decode happened is the point of this node's
    # fixture. `output.name` being the string "Ada Lovelace" and not { S: "Ada Lovelace" }
    # is the whole difference the encoding makes.
    output: "return output.found && output.output.name === 'Ada Lovelace'"
    found: "return output.found === true"
